column3: other meaning (only when the word means something else elsewhere)

column2: A system that starts in an energy eigenstate stays in the corresponding instantaneous eigenstate if its Hamiltonian changes slowly enough, provided an energy gap separates that state from the rest. It underpins adiabatic quantum computing and annealing.
A geometric phase a quantum state acquires when its Hamiltonian is slowly carried around a closed loop in parameter space. It depends only on the path's geometry, not on how long the trip takes.

An expansion of the time-evolution operator as a series of time-ordered integrals of the Hamiltonian. It is used when the Hamiltonian changes in time and does not commute with itself at different times.

The theory of systems driven by a Hamiltonian that repeats periodically in time. Their evolution over one period is described by an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian, used to design driven gates and phases.
A phase acquired by a quantum state that depends only on the path it traces through state or parameter space, not on energy or time. The Berry phase is the best-known example.
The operator for a system's total energy. It sets how quantum states evolve in time through the Schrödinger equation, and its eigenvalues are the allowed energies.
column3: In classical mechanics it is the energy function of a system; in graph theory a Hamiltonian path visits every vertex once.

column2: A description of quantum mechanics in which states stay fixed and operators (observables) evolve in time. It gives the same predictions as the Schrödinger picture.

A description that splits the Hamiltonian into a simple part and an interaction, moving the simple part's evolution into the operators. Only the interaction then changes the state, which simplifies driven and perturbed systems.

A transition between two energy levels when a parameter sweeps them through an avoided crossing. The Landau–Zener formula gives the chance of jumping levels, which falls as the sweep slows or the gap widens.
The rotation of a spin's magnetic moment around an applied magnetic field at the Larmor frequency, set by the field strength. For a qubit it appears as its Bloch vector circling the field axis.
A way to write the time-evolution operator of a time-dependent Hamiltonian as the exponential of a series of nested commutators. Unlike the Dyson series it keeps the evolution unitary at every order.

The periodic swing of a two-level system between its ground and excited states under a resonant drive. Its frequency grows with drive strength, and it is used to calibrate qubit rotations such as the π pulse.
A reference frame that rotates at a chosen frequency, usually the qubit or drive frequency. In this frame fast oscillations disappear, so driven qubit dynamics look simple and nearly static.

An approximation that drops the rapidly oscillating terms of a driven system in the rotating frame, keeping only near-resonant ones. It is accurate when the drive is weak compared with the transition frequency.
The fundamental equation of quantum mechanics describing how a state changes in time: its rate of change equals the Hamiltonian acting on it, divided by iħ.
A description of quantum mechanics in which states evolve in time while operators stay fixed. It is the most common picture in quantum computing, where circuits act on states.
How a quantum state changes over time. For a closed system it is a unitary operator generated by the Hamiltonian; for an open system it also includes noise from the environment.
The change of a closed quantum system over time by a unitary operator, which preserves normalization and can always be reversed. Every ideal quantum gate is a unitary evolution.
The most classical information a receiver can extract about which state from an ensemble was sent, maximized over all measurements. The Holevo bound caps it.
The rule that processing cannot increase information: applying a channel to a system never raises its mutual information or relative entropy with another system.
An observable whose expectation value is non-negative for every separable state but negative for some entangled ones. Measuring a negative value proves entanglement without full tomography.
A set of operations in which separated parties act only on their own systems and exchange classical messages. It cannot create entanglement, so it is used to define and compare entanglement.

An entropy based on the most likely outcome: the negative logarithm of the largest probability. It measures how hard a value is to guess, which is why it matters for randomness extraction and cryptography.
A measure of how much knowing one system tells you about another. In quantum information it equals S(A) + S(B) − S(AB) and counts both classical and quantum correlations.
A test for entanglement: take the partial transpose of a density matrix and check for negative eigenvalues. A negative one proves entanglement; for 2×2 and 2×3 systems the test is also sufficient.
A measure of quantum correlations beyond entanglement: the difference between two versions of mutual information that agree classically. Some separable states still have nonzero discord.
A measure of how distinguishable one quantum state is from another, D(ρ‖σ) = Tr ρ(log ρ − log σ). It is not symmetric, but it never increases under noise, so it is widely used in proofs.
A family of entropies with a parameter α that includes the von Neumann (α→1), collision (α=2) and min-entropy (α→∞) as special cases. The α=2 case can be measured on quantum hardware.
The average uncertainty of a classical random variable, measured in bits. It sets the limit for compressing classical data and is the classical counterpart of von Neumann entropy.
A fundamental inequality for von Neumann entropy: S(ABC) + S(B) ≤ S(AB) + S(BC). Many results in quantum information theory, including the data processing inequality, follow from it.
The quantum version of Shannon entropy, S(ρ) = −Tr ρ log ρ. It is zero for pure states and, for a pure bipartite state, measures the entanglement between the two parts.
An extra qubit used to help a computation, for example to measure a syndrome, hold a temporary result or implement a gate. It is usually prepared in a known state and reset or discarded afterwards.
column3: In everyday English, an ancillary thing is simply an auxiliary or supporting one.

column2: The basis of four maximally entangled two-qubit Bell states. Measuring in it, called Bell measurement, is central to teleportation and entanglement swapping.
The postulate that the probability of a measurement outcome is the squared magnitude of the state's amplitude for that outcome. It connects the mathematics of quantum states to experimental results.
Rewriting a state or operator in terms of a different set of basis vectors. In circuits, a gate such as Hadamard before a measurement changes which basis is measured.
The standard measurement basis of qubits, |0⟩ and |1⟩, and their products for many qubits. It is the eigenbasis of the Pauli Z operator.
Another name for the Hadamard basis, |+⟩ and |−⟩, the eigenstates of Pauli X. The name comes from polarization, where these states are diagonally polarized light.
The experiment in which single particles pass through two slits and build up an interference pattern, showing wave-like superposition. Finding out which slit they used destroys the pattern.
The basis of number states |0⟩, |1⟩, |2⟩ …, each with a definite number of photons or excitations in a mode. It is the natural basis for bosonic modes and photonics.
The basis of |+⟩ and |−⟩, equal superpositions of |0⟩ and |1⟩ with plus and minus sign. The Hadamard gate maps the computational basis to it, and it is the eigenbasis of Pauli X.
Reading out a quantum system, which gives a classical result and generally changes the state. In quantum computing it usually means measuring qubits in the computational basis.
column3: In everyday English, measurement means finding a size or amount, without disturbing what is measured.

column2: The axiom stating how measurements work: outcomes follow the Born rule and the state is updated, or collapses, to match the result. It is one of the postulates of quantum mechanics.

The open question of how and why measurement produces a single definite outcome, when the Schrödinger equation alone evolves states smoothly and deterministically. Interpretations of quantum mechanics answer it differently.
Sets of bases in which any state from one basis gives equally likely outcomes when measured in another. The Z, X and Y bases of a qubit are an example, used in tomography and QKD.
The basis formed by the eigenstates of a Pauli operator, X, Y or Z. It also means expressing operators as sums of Pauli strings, which is how Hamiltonians and noise are often written.
The state of a system right after a measurement, updated to match the observed outcome. For a projective measurement it is the normalized projection of the old state onto that outcome.
A positive operator-valued measure: the most general quantum measurement, described by positive operators that sum to the identity. It covers noisy measurements and measurements using ancillas.
A measurement described by orthogonal projectors, such as measuring a qubit in the computational basis. Repeating it immediately gives the same result.
The slowing or freezing of a quantum system's evolution by frequent measurement, because each measurement keeps projecting it back to its original state.
Returning a qubit to a known state, usually |0⟩, so it can be used again. It can be done by measurement followed by a correction, or by actively removing energy from the qubit.
A symmetric, informationally complete POVM: d² measurement elements with equal pairwise overlaps. It gives optimal single-setting quantum state tomography.
A 1922 experiment in which silver atoms passing through an uneven magnetic field split into two discrete beams, revealing quantized spin. It is the classic picture of measuring a qubit.
The sudden change of a quantum state to the state matching a measurement result, as described by the measurement postulate. Whether collapse is physical is debated among interpretations.
A measurement that couples only weakly to the system, gaining little information per shot while disturbing the state only slightly. It is used for continuous monitoring and feedback.

A one-to-one correspondence between quantum channels and quantum states: applying a channel to half of a maximally entangled state gives its Choi state. It turns questions about channels into questions about states.
A linear map that keeps states valid even when it acts on part of a larger entangled system. Every physical quantum operation must be completely positive.
A completely positive, trace-preserving map: the mathematical description of any physical quantum channel, including noise. It is also called a quantum operation.
A set of operators {K_i} describing a quantum channel as ρ → Σ K_i ρ K_i†, with Σ K_i†K_i = I. Each operator can be read as one way the noise may act.
Writing a quantum channel as a sum over Kraus operators, ρ → Σ K_i ρ K_i†. Every CPTP map has one, though it is not unique.
The state of a subsystem, obtained by tracing out the rest with the partial trace. It is also called the reduced state.
Finding a pure state on a larger system whose partial trace equals a given mixed state. Every mixed state can be purified by adding a large enough reference system.
The operation that discards part of a composite system, leaving the reduced density matrix of what remains. It is the quantum version of averaging over (marginalizing) unobserved variables.
Representing a mixed state as part of a pure state on a bigger system, so that tracing out the extra part gives back the mixed state.
column3: In error correction, entanglement purification (or distillation) instead means improving noisy entangled pairs.

column2: The most general physical process on quantum states, a CPTP map. It covers unitary gates, noise, measurement with discarded outcomes and transmission through a medium.
column3: In communication, a quantum channel can also mean the physical link, such as an optical fibre, that carries qubits.

column2: The density matrix of a subsystem, obtained by the partial trace over the rest. If the whole system is entangled, the reduced state of a part is mixed.

A theorem showing that every quantum channel can be realized as a unitary on the system plus an environment, followed by discarding the environment. Noise is thus entanglement with an unseen environment.
A map that keeps the trace of a density matrix equal to one, so probabilities still add up to 1. Physical channels are trace-preserving; maps that include postselection are not.
An operator equal to minus its own conjugate transpose, A† = −A. Multiplying a Hermitian operator by i gives an anti-Hermitian one, as in the generator −iHt of time evolution.
The combination {A, B} = AB + BA of two operators. Pauli matrices anticommute with each other, and anticommutators are central to fermions and Majorana modes.
The combination [A, B] = AB − BA of two operators. It is zero when they commute, meaning they can be measured together and their order does not matter.
column3: In electrical engineering, a commutator is the rotating switch in some electric motors.

column2: Observables whose commutator is zero. They share a set of eigenstates, so they can be measured together without disturbing each other.
An eigenvalue shared by more than one independent eigenvector, as when two different states have the same energy. Degeneracy gives freedom to choose the basis within that subspace.
The operator ρ describing a quantum state in full, including mixed states, as a weighted sum of pure-state projectors. In a chosen basis it is written as a density matrix.
A state that an operator only rescales, without changing its direction: A|ψ⟩ = a|ψ⟩. Measuring an observable on its own eigenstate gives the matching eigenvalue with certainty.
The number a in A|ψ⟩ = a|ψ⟩, by which an operator rescales its eigenstate. The eigenvalues of an observable are its possible measurement results.
The average result of measuring an observable many times on the same state, ⟨A⟩ = ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩. Variational algorithms such as VQE minimize the expectation value of a Hamiltonian.
An operator equal to its own conjugate transpose, A = A†. Hermitian operators have real eigenvalues, so they represent observables such as energy.
The conjugate transpose of an operator, written A†: transpose the matrix and take the complex conjugate of each entry. It turns kets into bras and undoes unitaries, since U†U = I.
The operator I that leaves every state unchanged. In circuits it corresponds to doing nothing, though real hardware still adds noise during that idle time.

A vector space with a bracket operation, such as the commutator, that captures the generators of continuous transformations. The Lie algebra su(2), spanned by the Pauli matrices, generates all single-qubit rotations.
The exponential of a matrix, e^A = Σ A^k/k!. Unitary gates and time evolution are matrix exponentials, such as U = e^(−iHt).
An operator that commutes with its own conjugate transpose, AA† = A†A. Normal operators, which include Hermitian and unitary ones, can be diagonalized in an orthonormal basis.
A measurable physical quantity, such as energy, spin or position, represented by a Hermitian operator whose eigenvalues are the possible results.
column3: In everyday English, observable just means able to be seen or noticed.

column2: A linear map acting on quantum states, usually written as a matrix. Gates, observables, Hamiltonians and density matrices are all operators.
column3: In everyday English, an operator is a person or company that runs a machine or service.

column2: The three 2×2 matrices X, Y and Z, which together with the identity form a basis for all single-qubit operators. They represent bit flips, phase flips and spin measurements.
The Pauli matrix that swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩, acting as the quantum NOT or bit-flip gate. It rotates the Bloch sphere by 180° about the X axis.
The Pauli matrix that flips the bit and adds a phase, mapping |0⟩ to i|1⟩ and |1⟩ to −i|0⟩. It rotates the Bloch sphere by 180° about the Y axis.
The Pauli matrix that leaves |0⟩ alone and flips the sign of |1⟩, acting as the phase-flip gate. Its eigenstates, |0⟩ and |1⟩, form the computational basis.
A Hermitian operator whose eigenvalues are all zero or positive, so ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩ ≥ 0 for every state. Density matrices and POVM elements must be positive semidefinite.
An operator that satisfies P² = P and projects states onto a subspace, such as |0⟩⟨0|. Projective measurements are described by sets of projectors that sum to the identity.
column3: In everyday English, a projector is a device that casts images onto a screen.

column2: The group of unitary matrices with determinant 1, written SU(n). Single-qubit gates correspond to SU(2), up to a global phase.
Writing a normal operator as a sum of its eigenvalues times projectors onto the matching eigenstates, A = Σ λ_i |i⟩⟨i|. It makes functions of operators, such as exponentials, easy to compute.
The limit on how precisely two non-commuting observables, such as position and momentum or X and Z, can both be known. The product of their spreads has a lower bound.
An operator whose conjugate transpose is its inverse, U†U = I. Unitaries preserve lengths and probabilities and are reversible; every ideal quantum gate is unitary.
column3: In politics, a unitary state is a country governed as a single unit.

column2: The spread of measurement results around their average, ⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩². It sets how many measurements (shots) are needed to estimate an expectation value precisely.
One of four maximally entangled two-qubit states, such as (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. Measuring one qubit fixes the other's result, and Bell states are the basic resource for teleportation and QKD.
A sphere representing every state of one qubit: pure states lie on the surface, mixed states inside. The poles are |0⟩ and |1⟩, and gates act as rotations of the sphere.
The arrow from the centre of the Bloch sphere to a qubit's state, with components equal to the expectation values of X, Y and Z. Its length is 1 for pure states and less for mixed states.
The row vector ⟨ψ| in Dirac notation, the conjugate transpose of the ket |ψ⟩. Combining a bra and a ket, ⟨φ|ψ⟩, gives an inner product.
A superposition of two very different states, such as all qubits in 0 and all in 1, or two opposite coherent states of light. It is named after Schrödinger's cat.
A highly entangled state on a lattice of qubits, made by preparing each in |+⟩ and applying CZ gates between neighbours. It is the resource for measurement-based quantum computing.
The quantum state closest to a classical wave, such as ideal laser light. It is an eigenstate of the annihilation operator and has a Poisson spread of photon numbers.
The complex number attached to each basis state in a superposition. Its squared magnitude gives the probability of that outcome, and its phase is what makes interference possible.
The matrix form of the density operator ρ, which describes any quantum state, pure or mixed. Its diagonal holds outcome probabilities and its off-diagonal entries hold coherences.
An equal superposition of all states of n qubits with exactly k of them in |1⟩. It is symmetric under swapping qubits and useful in metrology and some algorithms.
The bra-ket notation for quantum states: |ψ⟩ for a state (ket), ⟨ψ| for its conjugate (bra), and ⟨φ|ψ⟩ for their inner product. It is the standard language of quantum mechanics.
A correlation between quantum systems so strong that the whole cannot be described by describing each part separately. It has no classical equivalent and is a key resource in quantum computing.
column3: In everyday English, entanglement means being tangled up or caught in a complicated situation.

column2: Any state with more energy than the ground state. For a qubit it is usually |1⟩, which can decay back to |0⟩ by losing energy (T1 relaxation).
A state with an exact number of photons or excitations in a mode, written |n⟩. Unlike laser light, it has no uncertainty in photon number.
The Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger state (|00…0⟩ + |11…1⟩)/√2, a maximally entangled state of three or more qubits. It is used to benchmark hardware and to test quantum nonlocality.
The thermal equilibrium state of a system at a given temperature, ρ ∝ e^(−H/kT). Preparing Gibbs states is a task for quantum simulation algorithms.
A phase factor multiplying an entire state. It changes no measurement result and is physically unobservable, so states that differ only by a global phase are considered the same.
A multi-qubit entangled state defined by a graph: each vertex is a qubit in |+⟩, and each edge applies a CZ gate. Cluster states are graph states on a lattice.
The lowest-energy state of a system. Many algorithms, such as VQE and quantum phase estimation, aim to find a molecule's or material's ground state and its energy.
The complex vector space, with an inner product, in which quantum states live. For n qubits it has 2^n dimensions, which is why simulating qubits classically becomes hard.
column3: In mathematics, Hilbert spaces are also studied in their own right, well beyond quantum mechanics.

column2: The operation ⟨φ|ψ⟩ that takes two states and gives a complex number measuring their overlap. Its squared magnitude is the probability of finding state ψ when measuring for φ.
The column vector |ψ⟩ representing a quantum state in Dirac notation. For example, |0⟩ and |1⟩ are the kets of a qubit's basis states.
A state with the most entanglement possible for its size, such as a Bell state. Each part on its own is completely random (maximally mixed), while the whole is pure.
A state that is a probabilistic mixture of pure states, described by a density matrix. It arises from classical uncertainty, noise, or entanglement with a system you cannot see.
The requirement that the probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1, so a state's squared amplitudes sum to one. After a measurement or projection, the state is normalized again.
column3: In statistics and databases, normalization means rescaling or restructuring data.

column2: The operator |ψ⟩⟨φ| formed from a ket and a bra. The outer product of a state with itself, |ψ⟩⟨ψ|, is its density matrix and a projector.
The complex angle of an amplitude. Phases between basis states (relative phase) cause interference and matter; a phase on the whole state (global phase) does not.
column3: In everyday English a phase is a stage; in physics it can also mean a state of matter, such as solid or liquid.

column2: A multi-qubit state that can be written as a tensor product of individual qubit states, with no entanglement between them.
A quantum state described by a single state vector, with the most information possible. Its density matrix has purity 1, and on the Bloch sphere it sits on the surface.

A quantum bit, the basic unit of quantum information: a two-level system that can be in |0⟩, |1⟩ or any superposition of them. It can be built from superconducting circuits, ions, atoms, photons and more.
A quantum system with d levels instead of two, the generalization of a qubit. Qutrits (d = 3) are an example, and some hardware can use more than two levels per element.
A single mode of a quantum field, such as one mode of light, used as the basic unit of continuous-variable quantum computing. Its state lives in an infinite-dimensional space.
A three-level quantum system, with basis states |0⟩, |1⟩ and |2⟩. Qutrits can store more information per element and appear naturally in hardware such as transmons.
The phase difference between the amplitudes of basis states in a superposition, such as between (|0⟩ + |1⟩) and (|0⟩ − |1⟩). Unlike global phase it is measurable and drives interference.
Writing a two-part pure state as a sum of products of orthonormal states, Σ λ_i |a_i⟩|b_i⟩. The number of terms and the coefficients reveal how entangled the parts are.
The number of nonzero terms in a Schmidt decomposition. A rank of 1 means a product state; any higher rank means the state is entangled.
A state that can be written as a mixture of product states, and so is not entangled. All correlations in a separable state can be explained classically.
A particle with spin 1/2, such as an electron, whose spin along any axis measures as up or down. It is a natural qubit, and qubits are often described using spin language.

A state of light or a mode in which the uncertainty in one quadrature is reduced below the vacuum level at the cost of more in the other. Squeezing improves sensitivity, for example in gravitational-wave detectors.
The vector |ψ⟩ that fully describes a pure quantum state, listing the complex amplitudes of all basis states. For n qubits it holds 2^n amplitudes.
A combination of basis states with complex amplitudes, such as α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. A qubit in superposition is not in 0 or 1 until measured, when the amplitudes set the odds.
column3: In geology and in everyday use, superposition means placing one thing on top of another.

column2: The operation that combines state spaces of separate systems into one, written ⊗. The state of two qubits lives in the tensor product of two single-qubit spaces, with four dimensions.
A state in thermal equilibrium at a given temperature, with levels occupied according to Boltzmann weights. Qubits that are not cooled enough start partly in a thermal state instead of |0⟩.
The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix. For a density matrix it equals 1, and expectation values are computed as traces, ⟨A⟩ = Tr(ρA).
column3: In everyday English, a trace is a small mark or sign left behind.

column2: A quantum system with two energy levels, the physical basis of a qubit. In hardware, TLS also means unwanted two-level defects in materials, a major source of noise in superconducting qubits.
The three-qubit entangled state (|001⟩ + |010⟩ + |100⟩)/√3 and its larger versions. Unlike the GHZ state, it keeps some entanglement if one qubit is lost.
A mixture of a maximally entangled state with white noise, controlled by a single parameter. It is a standard example showing that entangled states need not violate a Bell inequality.
An inequality that every local hidden-variable theory must satisfy. Quantum mechanics predicts violations, which experiments have confirmed, ruling out local realism.
John Bell's 1964 result that no theory with local hidden variables can reproduce all predictions of quantum mechanics. It turned a philosophical debate into an experimental test.
The Clauser–Horne–Shimony–Holt inequality, the most widely tested Bell inequality: local theories give at most 2, while quantum mechanics reaches 2√2. It is used in device-independent protocols.

The 1935 argument by Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen that quantum mechanics must be incomplete, using entangled particles whose results are perfectly correlated. Bell's theorem later showed local hidden variables cannot explain these correlations.
A theorem showing that, in spaces of dimension three or more, any consistent assignment of probabilities to measurement outcomes must come from a density matrix via the Born rule.

A theory proposing that quantum results are fixed by unseen variables, making randomness only apparent. Bell's theorem rules out local versions; nonlocal ones, like Bohmian mechanics, remain possible.
The limit on how much classical information can be sent using quantum states: n qubits carry at most n classical bits, even though describing them takes 2^n amplitudes.
A theorem showing that quantum measurement results cannot all be fixed in advance independently of which other compatible measurements are made. It is the foundation of quantum contextuality.
The rule that entanglement cannot be freely shared: if two qubits are maximally entangled, neither can be entangled with a third. It underpins the security of quantum key distribution.
The result that the state of an unknown mixed system cannot be copied into two systems that each hold the original state. It extends the no-cloning theorem to mixed states.
The theorem that an unknown quantum state cannot be copied exactly. It forbids simple backups of qubits, secures quantum cryptography, and is why error correction must work indirectly.
The result that measuring one half of an entangled pair cannot send information to whoever holds the other half. Entanglement cannot be used for faster-than-light signalling.
The counterpart of no-cloning: given two copies of an unknown quantum state, one cannot be deleted against the other while leaving the first untouched.
The requirement that no action on one system can instantly change measurement statistics of a distant system. Quantum mechanics respects it despite entanglement.
The property that a measurement's result can depend on which other compatible measurements are made alongside it. It is a resource behind the power of some quantum computations.
Correlations between distant entangled systems that no local hidden-variable theory can explain, shown by violating Bell inequalities. It does not allow faster-than-light signalling.
The largest value quantum mechanics allows for the CHSH combination: 2√2, above the classical limit of 2 but below the no-signalling maximum of 4.
